name: Natural TRT / "enclo + hCG" protocols

lead: "Natural TRT" is a community label for raising the body's own testosterone rather than replacing it with injected testosterone. The usual tools are enclomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), with the appeal of keeping sperm production and testicular function while gaining the muscle and leanness higher testosterone brings.

Enclomiphene blocks estrogen's negative feedback at the pituitary, raising LH and FSH and so testicular testosterone output. hCG acts on the testes' LH receptor and stimulates testosterone without suppressing sperm production. Medical sources describe hCG and clomiphene-type drugs as alternatives for some men with low testosterone; enclomiphene never received marketing approval.

paras: Men typically use these under a clinician's supervision, often through hormone clinics, with bloodwork before and during use. They are discussed as alternatives to standard TRT for men who want to preserve fertility.

Enclomiphene safety data in 1,403 participants listed headache, hot flush and nausea, with rare thromboembolic events and one fatal stroke. The EU's CHMP recommended refusing authorisation in 2018 and development was discontinued in 2021. It is not approved in the US or EU; hCG and SERMs are prescription drugs, and products sold online outside medical supervision are not regulated for quality.

angle.text: Natural TRT protocols use enclomiphene and hCG to raise a man's own testosterone while keeping fertility, aiming for the muscle and leanness higher testosterone supports. Evidence for enclomiphene is limited and it never received marketing approval.

lead: 'Natural TRT' (also 'enclo + hCG', non-suppressive TRT) is a community label for approaches that aim to raise a man's own testosterone by stimulating the pituitary-testicular axis rather than replacing testosterone with an injected or topical dose. The two drugs most often named are enclomiphene (enclomifene), a nonsteroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a gonadotropin that mimics luteinizing hormone (LH).[1][2][3] Clomiphene, the parent drug of enclomiphene, belongs to the same conversation.[4]

The appearance case, as proponents put it, runs through testosterone: higher levels are associated with muscle mass, leaner body composition, energy for training, libido and androgen-linked traits, and doing it through the body's own signalling is meant to keep testicular size, sperm production and fertility intact.[5][6] Exogenous testosterone can suppress spermatogenesis, which is why fertility-preserving options draw interest among men who want to conceive later.[5][2]

Clinical sources describe hCG and low-dose clomifene as alternatives to replacement for some men with hypogonadism, particularly when fertility matters.[2][4] Enclomiphene was developed for secondary hypogonadism but never obtained marketing approval: the European Medicines Agency's committee recommended refusing authorisation in 2018 and development stopped for all indications in 2021.[1] In bodybuilding the hCG half of the pairing is a long-standing component of post-cycle recovery routines, and on looksmax.org enclomiphene is discussed as a way of 'testosterone maxxing', including threads by teenage users, a pattern that sits alongside Wikipedia's note that hCG use in adolescents needs close monitoring for early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure.[3][7][8][9]

paras: Enclomifene is the (E)-stereoisomer of clomifene, which is about 62 percent enclomifene and 38 percent zuclomifene; enclomifene is the more antiestrogenic of the two and zuclomifene the more estrogenic.[1][4] By blocking estrogen's negative feedback at the pituitary and hypothalamus it raises gonadotropin secretion and thereby testicular testosterone production.[1][4] Wikipedia describes enclomifene as studied mainly for men with secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and, unlike testosterone replacement, not linked to reduced spermatogenesis.[1]

In secondary hypogonadism, where LH and FSH are normal or low, the testes can respond to gonadotropin stimulation; in primary hypogonadism LH is usually elevated and the testes themselves are impaired, so the approach is described as ineffective in true testicular failure.[2] Men's total testosterone is generally taken as normal at about 240 to 950 ng/dL depending on age, with treatment often considered for symptomatic values below about 230 ng/dL, and the Endocrine Society did not recommend screening men without symptoms as of 2018.[2]

Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the LH receptor on testicular Leydig cells and stimulates testosterone production, which in turn supports sperm production. It is used medically in some forms of hypogonadism, alone or alongside testosterone, and to treat or prevent infertility, including during testosterone replacement, where it helps preserve fertility and prevent testicular atrophy.[3][2]

Wikipedia lists cautions: prolonged treatment can increase androgen production, men with androgen-dependent tumours should not take it, and teenagers need close monitoring for early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure.[3] In bodybuilding, hCG is commonly used during and after anabolic steroid cycles to maintain testicular size and natural testosterone output.[3] It appears on some sports' banned lists, and athletes including baseball's Manny Ramirez (50-game ban, 2009) and the NFL's Brian Cushing have been sanctioned.[3]

A separate use of hCG, the 'hCG diet', paired low-dose hCG with a very-low-calorie diet from the 1950s; Wikipedia reports that a 1976 study and a 1995 meta-analysis found no advantage over dietary restriction, that the FDA and FTC moved against unapproved hCG weight-loss products in December 2011, and that the AMA in 2016 called its use for weight loss inappropriate.[3]

Clomifene was synthesised by Merrell chemists in 1956, patented in 1959 and approved in the United States in 1967 as Clomid for female infertility; use in men is off-label.[4] Wikipedia notes that at typical doses it roughly doubles to 2.5 times testosterone in hypogonadal men, that enclomifene clears in about 10 hours while zuclomifene lingers for days to weeks, and that a purified enclomifene product was reported to be about twice as effective at raising testosterone.[4] The hypogonadism article describes low-dose clomiphene as an alternative to replacement that avoids infertility and generally has few side effects at those doses.[2]

Wikipedia cites a 2013 comparison of oral enclomiphene with testosterone gel that reported maintained sperm counts alongside raised testosterone, and a 2014 study reporting that enclomiphene raised serum testosterone within 14 days in men with low testosterone.[1] Safety data from 1,403 participants in phase 2 and 3 studies listed headache (1.6 percent), hot flush (1.1 percent) and nausea (1.0 percent), with rarer events including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and one fatal ischemic stroke.[1] Wikipedia's clomifene article reports one large study in which 25 mg a day raised low testosterone from 309 to 642 ng/dL over three months, with total cholesterol falling and HDL, triglycerides, glucose and prolactin unchanged.[4] No published trial of an enclomiphene plus hCG combination was identified.

Enclomiphene was developed as Androxal and EnCyzix for male hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes. It was under FDA and EMA review by December 2016, the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorisation in January 2018, and development was discontinued for all indications in April 2021.[1] Clomifene citrate is FDA-approved for ovulatory infertility and male use is off-label; WADA bans clomifene, and it can appear as an undeclared ingredient in black-market products.[4] hCG is a prescription drug; non-prescription hCG weight-loss products were targeted by US regulators in 2011.[3]

Wikipedia describes testosterone replacement as the classic treatment for male hypogonadism, with effects on libido and modest gains in physical activity and mood, and possible effects on spermatogenesis, hematocrit and sleep apnea.[5] A 2025 FDA decision, after the TRAVERSE trial found no increased cardiovascular risk versus placebo in hypogonadal men over a median 33 months, removed a boxed warning for cardiovascular risk; long-term safety remains unknown.[5] Suppressed spermatogenesis, which can cause infertility, is among its documented effects.[5]

The hypogonadism article notes that TRT generally suppresses sperm production and that men who want to conceive may be offered hCG or clomiphene, with testosterone often used for primary hypogonadism in men not seeking fertility.[2] An American College of Physicians guideline from 2020, summarised there, suggests discussing TRT for sexual dysfunction and says it may not be recommended for other reasons.[2]

On looksmax.org, enclomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-maximising compound; one thread title claims it gives users testosterone in the 90th to 99th percentile, and another is framed as a complete guide to 'testosterone maxxing' for users who consider themselves late developers.[7][10] Other threads cover use at age 15 to 17, sourcing questions, stacking with other compounds and questions about estrogen levels. These discussions often come from minors, and clinical labelling for hCG flags adolescents as needing close monitoring.[3] Some users report adverse experiences, for example fatigue and sleepiness after taking it.[11] In a thread asking whether enclomiphene could help with height or bones, a reply said it would do little unless testosterone is low and that growth hormone, not testosterone or DHT, is what matters for bone growth.[12]
A T Nation thread on testosterone and attracting the opposite sex shows the broader forum context in which testosterone is linked to social and physical outcomes.[6]
